image.subject: Niall Ferguson, a British historian in his fifties, short greying hair, dark sport jacket over an open-collar shirt, seated at a wooden desk with books, sketching a small cluster of dots joined by lines on a notepad

storyboard.claim: Betweenness centrality is a foundational network measure of how much information must pass through a given node.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host at his desk sketching a network of dots and lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the new concept after the tower-and-square framing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines betweenness as the share of paths that run through a node.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, standing in a doorway between a quiet engineering room of desks and a noisy bright marketing office

storyboard.claim: A person with no high title can hold power by linking two clusters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure from behind in the doorway joining two separate office groups.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the abstract measure a human position.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the two clusters: introverted engineers and extroverted marketers.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a wooden table, books and a map, a small group of men in dark coats standing in a half-circle around it

storyboard.claim: The connector holds immense informal power that is invisible on the org chart.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lodge table where a half-circle of men gathers around a shared map.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Links the connector to the invisible square.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the connector role to the square outside the tower's formal hierarchy.

image.subject: a long office floor of desks seen from a glass walkway, workers seated in small clusters with one figure walking between them

storyboard.claim: The invisible square decides how the tower works day to day.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A long office floor with clusters of workers and one connecting walker.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the concept to everyday workplace effect.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the informal network operating inside a formal building.

storyboard.claim: The math of this network traces back to a puzzle in 1735.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large year number 1735 on a plain field.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from daily life to the historical origin of the math.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dates the origin of the network puzzle.

storyboard.claim: The city of Konigsberg in Prussia was built around the Pregel River.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Place card naming Konigsberg, Prussia.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the setting of the bridge puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Locates the river city and its two islands.

storyboard.claim: Two islands were linked to each other and the mainland by exactly seven bridges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three short list items naming the islands, bridges and walk.
storyboard.onScreenText: TWO ISLANDS / SEVEN BRIDGES / ONE WALK
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the city's physical layout.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact bridge count of seven.

storyboard.claim: Could a walk cross all seven bridges exactly once?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card asking if all seven can be crossed once.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the layout into the puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the exact question locals struggled with for years.

image.subject: an 18th-century ink map of the river city with two islands and seven bridges, spread on a candle-lit library table, no lettering

storyboard.claim: People walked in circles trying to solve the bridge problem for years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ink map of the river city with islands and seven bridges on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the physical puzzle the question refers to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the river, islands and bridges of Konigsberg.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with a stack of mathematics books, an open notebook covered in dots and lines, and a quill

storyboard.claim: Euler proved the walk impossible by inventing a new branch of mathematics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mathematics books and a notebook of dots and lines on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the mathematician who answered the puzzle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Euler and his new branch of mathematics.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with a folded city map pushed aside, an inkwell and a bare sheet of paper

storyboard.claim: Euler ignored the physical map, the island sizes and the bridge materials.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A folded map pushed aside on a bare table with a blank sheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how Euler's method differed.
storyboard.addedInformation: States that size and material of the bridges did not matter.

storyboard.claim: Euler reduced the city to nodes, the land masses, and edges, the bridges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows from stripping away physical detail.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the two abstract parts of a network.

left.label: LAND MASSES
left.subject: a pen-and-ink map of two river islands joined to the banks by seven bridges on a library table

right.label: NODES AND EDGES
right.subject: the same islands reduced to a few dots joined by plain lines on a blank sheet of paper

storyboard.claim: The city becomes a graph of nodes and edges.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Left, the islands and bridges as drawn land; right, the same as dots and lines.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the abstraction from the previous line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Pairs the physical city with its graph reduction.

image.subject: a sheet of graph paper on a wooden table with a few dots joined by lines, one dot circled in ink, beside a candle

storyboard.claim: A walk needs a graph with exactly two nodes of odd degree or none.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Graph paper with dots and lines, one dot circled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the abstraction to the proof's condition.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the odd-degree condition for a continuous walk.

storyboard.claim: Entering and leaving a node needs an even number of edges unless it is the start or end.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only, conversational.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A conversational clarification of the proof.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains why even edge counts matter at each node.

storyboard.claim: Konigsberg had four land masses, each with an odd number of bridges, so the walk was impossible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three list items summarising the verdict.
storyboard.onScreenText: FOUR LAND MASSES / ODD BRIDGES / NO WALK
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the proof to Konigsberg.
storyboard.addedInformation: Confirms all four land masses have odd bridge counts.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind at a window, looking down on a crowded 18th-century street of pedestrians and carriages

storyboard.claim: If human behaviour reduces to nodes and edges, it might be fully controllable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Figure from behind at a window over a busy street.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the math to the question of human behaviour.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the naive assumption that networks can be engineered.

storyboard.claim: Does the map of human links mean behaviour is totally controllable?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card on the assumption.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Poses the question the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the contradiction with predictability.

image.subject: Mark Zuckerberg, a 21st-century American tech founder in his thirties, short brown hair, plain grey T-shirt under a dark hoodie, no tie, standing before a row of server racks in a cool data centre

storyboard.claim: Modern mappers like Facebook map friendships and believe they can control the network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zuckerberg before server racks in a data centre.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the mapping idea into the modern era.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Facebook as a modern mapper of social links.

image.subject: a wooden desk with a ledger, a closed book and a map pinned to a plaster wall, a single candle burning

storyboard.claim: Engineering the links assumes the network is predictable, which the math contradicts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Desk with ledger, book and map under a candle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the control assumption.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the claim that the network is not predictable.

storyboard.claim: Why are social networks unstable, and why do revolutions happen overnight?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Question card asking about instability and overnight revolutions.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the paradox from the contradiction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames instability and sudden revolution as the puzzle.

image.subject: a printed sociogram on paper, dots and lines spread across a wooden table in a candle-lit library, beside a map and a ledger

storyboard.claim: We can map the current structure of nodes, but the network also has emergent properties.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sociogram diagram on paper on a library table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Acknowledges the sociogram before adding dynamics.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces sociograms as a way to draw current structure.

storyboard.claim: A human social network is dynamic and constantly shifting, not a static stone bridge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the difference from a physical bridge.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts a static bridge with a shifting human network.

image.subject: a stone square at dusk with two separate groups of people on either side of a narrow gap, one thin strand of light crossing the gap

storyboard.claim: A single new connection between two clusters can cause a massive phase transition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two groups in a square divided by a gap, one strand of light crossing it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the dynamic claim a visible form.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the trigger as one link between separate clusters.

image.subject: a candle-lit dining table in an 18th-century room with a dozen guests in small clusters, each deep in a separate low-voiced conversation

storyboard.claim: A quiet dinner party has several disconnected clusters talking separately.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dining table with guests in separate clusters.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the abstract clusters in a familiar scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows multiple disconnected clusters in one room.

image.subject: an ordinary person of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, leaning into a dinner table to speak loudly across two groups of seated guests

storyboard.claim: A shocking piece of gossip, loud enough for two groups to hear, bridges them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Figure from behind leaning across two seated groups.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the bridging event to the dinner scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the bridging act as one person speaking across groups.

image.subject: a candle-lit dinner room where all the guests have turned toward one table, forming a single close circle

storyboard.claim: Every person stops and joins one highly charged unified conversation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Guests turned into one circle around a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the result of the gossip crossing the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the merged group after the bridge forms.

storyboard.claim: The whole room's structure changed in one second from one new piece of information.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large stat: 1 SECOND.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quantifies the speed of the transition.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the transition took one second.

image.subject: Henry Kissinger, an elderly American statesman in a dark suit, white hair combed back, heavy-framed glasses, seated at a long table in a stone room with papers spread before him

storyboard.claim: The tower believes it perfectly controls its environment, until a rumour crosses a weak tie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Kissinger seated at a long table with papers in a stone room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the room to the tower's view of control.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places a statesman who invoked networks as the tower's voice.

image.subject: a folded letter passed from hand to hand across a crowded 19th-century city square

storyboard.claim: A rumour spreads across a weak tie and the structure collapses.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Folded letter passed hand to hand in a crowded square.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the weak tie a visible carrier.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows a weak tie carrying information across a crowd.

image.subject: a large, peaceful crowd filling a city square at dusk, people with their backs to the camera, no readable banners

storyboard.claim: The Arab Spring is a modern example of a massive phase transition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large peaceful crowd filling a city square at dusk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the phase transition a modern example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the Arab Spring as the modern case.

image.subject: a scholar in a candle-lit library reading a ledger, a stack of books and loose papers beside him on a wooden table

storyboard.claim: Networks cannot be neatly engineered the way hierarchies are engineered.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Scholar reading a ledger in a library.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Draws the conclusion from the examples.
storyboard.addedInformation: States that networks are inherently unpredictable, unlike hierarchies.

image.subject: a tall stone tower with narrow windows seen from the square below, a crowd of people milling beneath it

storyboard.claim: The tower looks down at the square's chaotic web of shifting alliances and panics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stone tower viewed from a crowded square below.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the tower-and-square metaphor.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the institutional fear of the unpredictable square.

image.subject: a candle-lit library table with an open folio, loose papers and a closed ledger beside a dark window

storyboard.claim: The next beat is the myth of the omnipotent network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Open folio and papers on a library table by a dark window.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridges to the next myth beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the myth that the next beat examines.

storyboard.claim: When the tower gets scared, it starts seeing ghosts, so we go to the early 1900s.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Statement text only as the time transition.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the myth to the historical case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the early 1900s as the example period.

image.subject: a smoke-filled private club in London, men in deep leather armchairs around a low table with glasses of port, seen from the doorway

storyboard.claim: A posh London club is where the early-1900s planning happens.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Smoke-filled club with leather armchairs and port glasses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves to the historical setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the scene in a London club in the early 1900s.

image.subject: a grey-haired British man in a dark Edwardian suit seated in a leather armchair in a smoke-filled club, a notebook on his knee

storyboard.claim: Lord Alfred Milner's so-called kindergarten, later the round table, meets here.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Edwardian man in a leather armchair with a notebook.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the group in the club.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names Milner and his kindergarten group.

image.subject: an ordinary early-1900s British man in a dark tailored suit, seen from behind, leaning over a notebook in a leather armchair

storyboard.claim: They were young, ambitious, highly educated British imperialists, including writers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Edwardian man from behind taking notes in a leather armchair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the members of the group.
storyboard.addedInformation: Characterises the young British imperialists.

image.subject: four men in dark suits in a smoke-filled club, seated in leather armchairs around a low table, one writing notes, port glasses on the table

storyboard.claim: They were the intellectual elite of the Edwardian era, dreaming aloud of a massive empire.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Four men in leather armchairs around port glasses, one writing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the group dreaming in the club.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the group as the intellectual elite of the era.

image.subject: an early-1900s world map hung on a club wall with Britain, America and the Dominions shaded in one colour, no lettering

storyboard.claim: They wanted a federal English-speaking world empire run essentially from London.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Early-1900s world map with Britain, America and the Dominions shaded alike.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the imperial vision a map.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the goal as a federal empire uniting the UK, America and the Dominions.
